## Memory and Communication at Training Scale {#sec-ch5}

*What Fills the Memory, What Crosses the Wire, and What That Costs*

### Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

- Name every category that occupies accelerator memory during
  training, and distinguish a logical/theoretical memory estimate
  from a measured peak-allocated value.
- Derive a per-parameter memory accounting for a given precision and
  optimizer, and state how data parallelism versus ZeRO/FSDP sharding
  changes residency without changing which objects exist.
- State why activation memory cannot be inferred from parameter count
  alone, and name the variables it actually depends on.
- Compute a collective's communication payload and distinguish payload
  volume from wall-clock communication time.
- Use a simple latency-bandwidth cost model to estimate communication
  time, and state why nominal link bandwidth is not the same as
  effective application bandwidth.
- Distinguish exposed from hidden communication, and explain why
  overlap reduces exposed time without making communication free.
- Diagnose, from a short list of symptoms, which resource (compute,
  memory bandwidth, interconnect bandwidth, or a scheduling bubble)
  most plausibly bounds a given training step's throughput.

### Why this matters

Chapter 4 established what data parallelism, ZeRO/FSDP, tensor
parallelism, sequence/context parallelism, pipeline parallelism, and
expert parallelism each replicate, shard, and communicate. This
chapter does not reteach those mechanisms. Its job is the next
question every one of them raises in practice: given a specific model,
cluster, and parallelism configuration, will it actually fit in
memory, and will communication actually slow it down — and by how
much? Answering "it depends on the configuration" is not useful on its
own; this chapter gives the accounting and the cost model that turn
"it depends" into an actual number, together with the discipline to
label every such number as an estimate or a measurement, never both.

### Mental model or analogy

::: {.callout-note title="Analogy"}
Picture a kitchen with a fixed amount of counter space (accelerator
memory) and a conveyor belt to a shared pantry down the hall
(interconnect bandwidth). Some items must sit on the counter the whole
shift — the recipe cards, the master ingredient list (model
parameters, optimizer state). Some items pile up and get cleared as
each dish finishes (activations). Walking to the pantry takes a fixed
amount of time per trip plus more time for a bigger order (the
latency-bandwidth cost model) — and if a cook can keep chopping while
a runner fetches the next order, that walk is "hidden"; if everyone
has to stop and wait for the runner, it is "exposed." **Where this
breaks down:** a real accelerator's "runner" (communication kernels)
and "cook" (compute kernels) often share the same hands — the same
streaming multiprocessors — so a walk to the pantry is never perfectly
free even when it overlaps with chopping, just cheaper than stopping
entirely.
:::

### Technical core

**Memory taxonomy: what actually occupies accelerator memory.**
Training memory is not one number. The items that occupy it are:
parameters; gradients; optimizer states; a mixed-precision master-weight
copy of the parameters (and sometimes of the gradients); saved
activations needed for the backward pass; temporary workspaces a
kernel allocates transiently; communication buffers (contiguous
staging memory a collective needs, which itself "contributes in part
to the peak memory usage during training" [@src-17]); and
fragmentation/runtime overhead the allocator cannot fully pack. A
separate axis distinguishes *how confidently* a number describes any
of these: **logical tensor memory** (the exact byte count a tensor's
shape and dtype imply); a **theoretical lower bound** (logical memory
under a stated, idealized sharding/recomputation policy); an
**estimated peak** (a formula applied to a configuration, as in this
chapter's own worked example below); and **measured peak
allocated/reserved memory** (what a profiler or `nvidia-smi` actually
reports for a real run, which includes the allocator's own
fragmentation and reserved-but-unused blocks [@src-17]). Every number
in this chapter is one of the first three kinds — a calculation — not
the fourth. There is no single "bytes per parameter" constant: the
right multiplier depends on precision and on which optimizer states
exist, declared explicitly every time below.

**Model-state memory: parameters, gradients, optimizer states.** For
a transformer with hidden size $h$, vocabulary size $v$, and $L$
layers, the non-embedding-adjusted parameter count is

$$
N = h \cdot v + L \cdot (12h^2 + 13h) + 2h
$$ {#eq-param-count}

[@src-17]. In mixed-precision training (BF16 compute, FP32 "master
weight" copy, Adam momentum and variance in FP32, no separate FP32
gradient accumulation), the per-rank memory for the four model-state
objects is

$$
m_{\text{params}} = 2N, \quad m_{\text{grad}} = 2N, \quad m_{\text{params\_fp32}} = 4N, \quad m_{\text{opt}} = 8N
$$ {#eq-model-state-bytes}

summing to $16N$ bytes [@src-17]. Under **vanilla data parallelism**,
every one of these four objects is fully replicated on every rank — a
real memory redundancy, not a design requirement. **ZeRO-3/FSDP**
partitions all four across the data-parallel group of size $N_d$,
reducing each rank's share to $16N/N_d$ bytes — the ZeRO paper's own
notation bundles the master-weight and optimizer terms into a single
"$k\Psi$" term with $k=12$ for mixed-precision Adam (here,
$4N + 8N = 12N$), a coarser bookkeeping than the Playbook's four-way
split but the same total [@src-54;@src-17]. Sharding changes *where*
each object's bytes live and *what* must be communicated to
reconstruct them when needed — it does not add, remove, or redefine
any of the four objects themselves, and it does not change the
mathematical quantity the optimizer is computing.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common misconception"}
**"Mixed precision roughly halves total training memory versus full
FP32."** It does not. Full FP32 training needs $4N + 4N + 8N = 16N$
bytes (params, gradients, optimizer states); mixed precision needs
$2N + 2N + 4N + 8N = 16N$ bytes — the *same* total, just redistributed
across more objects, because the FP32 master-weight copy adds back
what BF16 saved on the live parameters and gradients [@src-17]. Mixed
precision's real benefit is faster, lower-memory *activations* and
faster compute kernels, not a smaller model-state total.
:::

**Activation memory depends on far more than parameter count.** For a
microbatch size $bs$, sequence length $seq$, hidden size $h$, layer
count $L$, and attention head count $n_{\text{heads}}$, mixed-precision
activation memory is

$$
m_{\text{act}} = L \cdot seq \cdot bs \cdot h \cdot \left(34 + \frac{5 \cdot n_{\text{heads}} \cdot seq}{h}\right)
$$ {#eq-activation-memory}

[@src-17]. This scales *linearly* with batch size but *quadratically*
with sequence length through the attention term — a model with twice
the parameters but the same $h$, $L$, $seq$, and $bs$ does not
automatically need twice the activation memory, and a model with the
same parameter count run at 4x the sequence length needs far more than
4x the activation memory. Parameter count alone determines none of
this. **Activation recomputation** (gradient checkpointing) trades
compute for memory: a **full** strategy checkpoints only at each
layer's boundary and recomputes everything between boundaries during
the backward pass, at "up to 30-40%" added compute cost [@src-17];
a **selective** strategy checkpoints the expensive feedforward
activations and recomputes only the cheap-to-redo attention
activations, reported for a GPT-3-175B-scale model as "70% activation
memory reduction at a 2.7% compute cost" [@src-17]. Pipeline
parallelism changes the picture again: GPipe's own peak-activation
analysis with re-materialization gives $O\left(N + \frac{L}{K}\cdot\frac{N}{M}\right)$
for a model with $L$ layers split into $K$ pipeline partitions and $M$
microbatches (where $N$ here is GPipe's own per-layer activation-size
notation, not this chapter's parameter count) — versus
$O(N \cdot L)$ with neither recomputation nor partitioning
[@src-52]. More pipeline stages and more microbatches both shrink this
peak, for different structural reasons.

**Communication primitives and their payload volumes.** Chapter 4
introduced which strategy uses which primitive; here is what each
primitive actually moves, in terms of a payload of $\Psi$ elements.
An **all-reduce** (vanilla DP's gradient sync) costs $2\Psi$ — ZeRO's
own accounting: it decomposes into a reduce-scatter ($\Psi$) followed
by an all-gather ($\Psi$) [@src-54]. A **reduce-scatter** or an
**all-gather** alone costs $\Psi$ each. Per training step, ZeRO's own
reported totals are: vanilla DP, $2\Psi$; ZeRO-2 ($P_{os+g}$, optimizer
state + gradient partitioning), *also* $2\Psi$ — "exactly the same as
the baseline DP" [@src-54]; ZeRO-3 ($P_{os+g+p}$, full parameter
partitioning too), $3\Psi$, "1.5x compared to the baseline"
[@src-54]. **All-to-all** (expert-parallel token routing) and
**point-to-point send/receive** (pipeline-parallel activation/gradient
handoff) do not fit this $\Psi$-per-rank accounting at all: their cost
depends on how tokens are routed or which two neighboring ranks are
exchanging data, not on an all-ranks-participate collective pattern.
The number of *participating devices* ($N_d$ in the formulas above),
the *payload size*, and the *wall-clock time* a collective takes are
three different quantities — the next section is about the last of
these.

**A communication cost model.** A simple latency-bandwidth model for
one collective or point-to-point transfer is

$$
T_{\text{comm}} \approx \alpha \cdot \text{(number of messages)} + \frac{\text{bytes moved}}{\text{effective bandwidth}}
$$ {#eq-comm-cost-model}

where $\alpha$ is a fixed per-message latency (independent of size) and
*effective bandwidth* is **not** a link's nominal/peak bandwidth — it
is whatever throughput the collective implementation, network topology,
and contention from other traffic actually deliver, and it must be
measured or conservatively assumed, never assumed equal to a
datasheet number. On real hardware, achieved compute throughput alone
already falls short of peak: "H100s and B200s can usually only achieve
around 80-85% of the claimed peak FLOPs, while TPUs can get closer to
95% in normal use" [@src-10] — the same caution applies to bandwidth.
The Ultra-Scale Playbook's own derivation applies this cost model
directly to each parallelism strategy's dominant collective, yielding
a *ratio* of communication time to compute time that must stay $\le 1$
for full overlap: for vanilla DP's gradient all-reduce, the ratio is
$\frac{N}{2 \cdot \text{tokens}} \cdot \frac{N_d-1}{N_d} \cdot \frac{\text{peak\_flops}}{\text{peak\_bw}}$;
for ZeRO-3's per-layer parameter all-gather,
$\frac{1}{2 \cdot seq \cdot bs} \cdot \frac{N_d-1}{N_d} \cdot \frac{\text{peak\_flops}}{\text{peak\_bw}}$;
for tensor parallelism's activation all-gather,
$\frac{TP-1}{2h} \cdot \frac{\text{peak\_flops}}{\text{peak\_bw}}$ — notably
independent of sequence length or batch size, depending only on $h$
and the TP degree; and for pipeline parallelism's point-to-point
activation handoff,
$\frac{\text{peak\_flops}}{32h \cdot L_{\text{next stage}} \cdot \text{peak\_bw}}$ —
also independent of sequence length and batch size [@src-17]. Each
ratio names exactly which configuration variables push a strategy
toward being communication-bound.

**Overlap hides communication; it does not make it free.** Real
implementations reduce exposed communication through **bucketing**
(grouping many small gradients into one larger message — "the default
bucket size is often around 25MB" [@src-17] — since one large transfer
amortizes the fixed per-message latency $\alpha$ better than many
small ones), **prefetching** (starting the next layer's parameter
all-gather while the current layer still computes, as ZeRO-3 does),
and **asynchronous collectives** that let compute proceed without
waiting. All of these reduce *exposed* time, not the underlying
*payload*, and all are constrained by real dependencies: a rank cannot
use a parameter it has not yet received, and cannot start a backward
pass on a layer whose forward activations were discarded and not yet
recomputed. Crucially, overlap is not free even when it succeeds:
communication kernels typically execute on the same GPU streaming
multiprocessors that compute kernels use, so "overlapping communication
with computation" shares a finite resource rather than using two
independent ones, which is exactly why real implementations see
"decreased throughput when communication is overlapped with
computation" relative to a naive estimate that assumes communication
is simply invisible [@src-17]. The critical path for a training step
is compute time plus *whatever communication could not be hidden* —
never less than compute time alone.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common misconception"}
**"If communication is fully overlapped, it doesn't affect step
time."** Fully *hidden* communication does not *extend* the critical
path, but it still occupies real GPU resources (SMs, memory bandwidth)
concurrently with compute, and it still required real engineering
(bucketing, prefetching, correctly ordered async calls) to hide.
"Overlapped" means "not on the critical path," not "did not happen."
:::

**Throughput and bottleneck diagnosis.** Tokens/second and
samples/second are *observed* metrics — read from a running job, not
computed in advance. Model FLOP utilization (MFU) compares the FLOPs a
model's forward-and-backward pass actually requires (excluding
recomputation) against the accelerator's peak FLOPs over the step's
wall-clock time; it is a measured-versus-theoretical *ratio*, not
either quantity alone. Whether a step is compute-bound or
bandwidth-bound can be read from its **arithmetic intensity** — "the
ratio of the total FLOPs [an operation] performs to the number of
bytes it needs to communicate," either within a chip (memory
bandwidth) or between chips (interconnect bandwidth) [@src-10]. An
operation is compute-bound when its own intensity exceeds the
hardware's own peak intensity (peak FLOPs/s divided by peak
bytes/s) [@src-10] — below that threshold, adding more FLOPs/s does not
help, because the bottleneck is how fast bytes can move, not how fast
they can be multiplied. The Ultra-Scale Playbook's own benchmarks
(several thousand configurations across up to 64 nodes) found
efficiency decreasing as node count increases, especially for smaller
models with a lower compute-to-communication ratio, and found that
*which* strategy (tensor versus pipeline parallelism) ran faster
depended on *implementation* quality, not just theory — "when we first
implemented both parallelism strategies, Tensor Parallelism (TP)
outperformed Pipeline Parallelism (PP). After optimizing our PP code,
it became the faster option" [@src-17]. Megatron-LM's own scaling
experiment shows the same bottleneck *shifting* within a single
measured run: "using two GPUs makes training 64% faster. Above that we
see diminishing returns as the per-GPU computation decreases and the
memory bandwidth and communication overheads begin to dominate"
[@src-53] — the bottleneck moved from compute to bandwidth as more
GPUs were added to the same fixed problem. **Pipeline bubbles**,
**load imbalance** (uneven work per stage or per rank), and
**stragglers** (one slow rank pacing everyone else) are separate
throughput limiters from a bandwidth bottleneck — diagnosing which one
applies requires looking at where idle time actually falls, not
assuming a single universal cause.

**Architecture shape and systems behavior are not the same axis.**
Two models with equal total parameter counts but different
depth/width allocations (more layers and a narrower hidden size, versus
fewer layers and a wider hidden size) need not behave equally as
systems problems, even before any data or measured benchmark enters
the discussion. Greater sequential depth means more pipeline stages
are structurally possible, but also a longer chain of strictly
sequential forward (and backward) steps per microbatch, which is
exactly what creates the fill/drain bubble Chapter 4 covered — a
deeper model offers more pipeline-partitioning opportunities at the
cost of more inherent sequential latency per token. A wider hidden
size changes the matrix dimensions inside every matmul: Megatron-LM's
own tensor-parallel communication ratio above depends only on $h$ and
the TP degree, so width directly changes how much TP communication a
fixed TP degree implies, independent of depth. Width also changes
per-layer activation residency directly (every term in
@eq-activation-memory scales with $h$), while depth changes how many
times that per-layer cost is paid. Neither "deeper" nor "wider" is
universally better for hardware utilization, latency, or throughput —
each shifts a different term in the equations above, and the right
allocation for a fixed parameter budget depends on which of those
terms is already the binding constraint for a given cluster and
sequence length.

### Worked example

**Setup — a toy configuration, not a real model or cluster.** Hidden
size $h=4096$, vocabulary $v=32{,}000$, $L=24$ layers,
$n_{\text{heads}}=32$, sequence length $seq=2048$, micro-batch size
$bs=2$, a data-parallel degree of 8 (equal to the toy world size, so
no other parallelism axis is active), and three declared, illustrative
assumptions: an effective interconnect bandwidth of 200 GB/s, a fixed
per-message latency $\alpha = 10\,\mu s$, and a step's pure compute
time of 120 ms. None of these numbers describes a measured run.

**Model-state memory, before and after sharding.** From
@eq-param-count, this configuration has $N \approx 4.96$ billion
parameters. From @eq-model-state-bytes, replicated (vanilla DP) model-state
memory per rank is 74.0 GiB — 9.2 GiB bf16 parameters, 9.2 GiB bf16
gradients, 18.5 GiB fp32 master weights, 37.0 GiB fp32 Adam state.
After ZeRO-3/FSDP sharding across the 8-way DP group, every one of
those four numbers is divided by 8: 9.2 GiB total per rank (1.2 GiB +
1.2 GiB + 2.3 GiB + 4.6 GiB) — the same four objects, an eighth of
each.

**One activation-memory estimate.** From @eq-activation-memory, this
configuration's activation memory without recomputation is 42.75 GiB
for one microbatch — already more than half of the replicated
model-state total, illustrating why activation memory cannot be
ignored even when parameter count alone looks "small." Applying the
general recomputation *principle* (store only each layer's boundary
activation, recompute the rest) to this same toy configuration gives
an illustrative boundary-only estimate of 0.75 GiB — a reduction of
more than 50x in this toy case, at the cost of redoing each layer's
forward pass during the backward pass. This specific reduced-case
number is this chapter's own script-computed application of the
source's stated principle, not a formula the source gives directly for
this exact case.

**Communication payload for one collective.** For ZeRO-3's per-block
forward-pass parameter all-gather, each rank's share of one
transformer block's $16h^2$ parameters is $16h^2/8$ elements, or 64 MiB
in bf16 — and 1536 MiB summed across all 24 blocks for one full
forward pass.

**Estimated communication time.** Using @eq-comm-cost-model with the
declared 200 GB/s effective bandwidth and $10\,\mu s$ per-message
latency, one block's all-gather takes an estimated 0.346 ms; summed
across 24 blocks, 8.29 ms of total communication for the forward
pass's parameter all-gathers.

**Exposed communication after a declared overlap fraction.** Declaring
that 70% of this communication is successfully hidden via prefetching
(an illustrative assumption, not a measured overlap rate) leaves 5.81 ms
hidden and 2.49 ms **exposed** — the portion that actually extends the
critical path.

**Resulting illustrative step-time impact.** Step time with this
overlap is compute (120 ms) plus exposed communication (2.49 ms) =
122.49 ms. Without any overlap at all, step time would be 120 ms plus
the *entire* 8.29 ms = 128.29 ms. Overlap's benefit in this toy
scenario is therefore about 4.5% — illustrative of the *mechanism*,
not a claim about what any real model's overlap actually saves.

**Invalid configurations are rejected.** The worked example's own
script rejects a DP degree that does not evenly divide the declared
world size, an overlap fraction outside $[0,1]$, a non-positive
effective bandwidth, and a head count that does not evenly divide the
hidden size — each confirmed to raise before any of the numbers above
are trusted.

### Compare and contrast

| Aspect | Vanilla DP | ZeRO-1 | ZeRO-2 | ZeRO-3/FSDP | TP (per layer) | PP (per stage) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Model-state mem/rank | $16N$ | $4N+\frac{12N}{N_d}$ | $2N+\frac{14N}{N_d}$ | $\frac{16N}{N_d}$ | $\approx\frac{16N}{TP}$\* | $\approx\frac{16N}{PP}$\* |
| Comm volume/step | $2\Psi$ | $2\Psi$ (same as DP) | $2\Psi$ (same as DP) | $3\Psi$ (1.5x DP) | per-layer, scales with $seq\cdot bs\cdot h$ | per-microbatch, scales with $seq\cdot bs\cdot h$ |
| Dominant pattern | all-reduce | reduce-scatter + all-gather | reduce-scatter + all-gather | on-demand param all-gather | all-reduce / all-gather | point-to-point send/recv |
| Overlap ratio depends on | tokens, $N_d$, peak flops/bw | same as DP | same as DP | $seq\cdot bs$, $N_d$, peak flops/bw | only $h$, $TP$ | only $h$, $L_{\text{next}}$ |
| Key constraint | redundant by design | — | — | extra 50% volume vs. baseline | ratio independent of $seq$/$bs$ | ratio independent of $seq$/$bs$ |

: Model-state memory and communication, compared across the strategies Chapter 4 introduced — not a claim about which is fastest in general, since that depends on $h$, $seq$, $bs$, and hardware bandwidth. \*TP/PP entries assume even partitioning across ranks/stages; real partitioning is rarely perfectly even. {#tbl-memory-comm-compare}

### Applied exercise

Using this chapter's own worked example as a template, redo the
communication-time and step-time calculation for a declared overlap
fraction of 0.4 instead of 0.7, keeping every other toy input the same
(the same 8.29 ms total communication and 120 ms compute time).
Compute the new exposed communication time, the new step time, and the
new overlap-benefit percentage relative to the fully-exposed case, and
confirm that a *lower* overlap fraction produces a *smaller* benefit
percentage than this chapter's own 4.5% — i.e. that less effective
overlap is strictly worse, not merely different.

### Interview lens

*"A model that fits in memory during a quick test OOMs once you start
real training. What would you check?"* A strong answer separates the
memory categories this chapter distinguishes rather than guessing: the
quick test likely ran forward-only or with a tiny batch, so it never
allocated the optimizer states (which only appear after the first
optimizer step) or the full activation memory a real batch size and
sequence length require — both of which this chapter's own formulas
show scale with factors a forward-only smoke test would not exercise.
A complete answer also distinguishes an *estimated* peak (computed
from the model's configuration) from a *measured* peak (what a
profiler actually reports, including fragmentation and allocator
overhead), and checks whether communication buffers for a newly added
parallelism strategy were accounted for. An answer that jumps straight
to "reduce batch size" without first identifying *which* memory
category grew is incomplete — it might work, but it does not explain
why the quick test passed.

### Chapter recap

- Training memory is not one number: parameters, gradients, optimizer
  states, master weights, activations, workspaces, communication
  buffers, and fragmentation are distinct categories, and a number
  describing any of them is either a logical count, a theoretical
  bound, an estimate, or a measurement — never more than one of those
  at once (@eq-param-count, @eq-model-state-bytes).
- Mixed precision does not reduce total model-state memory versus full
  FP32 (both are $16N$ bytes) — its benefit is in activations and
  compute speed, not a smaller optimizer footprint.
- Activation memory depends on sequence length, batch size, hidden
  size, layer count, and attention heads — not parameter count alone —
  and scales quadratically with sequence length through attention
  (@eq-activation-memory); recomputation trades compute for a large
  memory reduction, more dramatically under pipeline parallelism's own
  partition-aware formula.
- Payload volume, number of participating devices, and wall-clock
  communication time are three different quantities; ZeRO's own
  reported volumes show sharding stages do not all cost equally more
  communication (ZeRO-2 matches vanilla DP's $2\Psi$; only ZeRO-3 adds
  50%).
- A latency-bandwidth cost model (@eq-comm-cost-model) estimates
  communication time, but effective bandwidth is never the same as
  nominal/peak bandwidth, and overlap hides exposed time without
  making communication resource-free, since communication kernels
  typically share GPU execution resources with compute kernels.
- Diagnosing a throughput bottleneck means checking arithmetic
  intensity against hardware's own peak intensity, and distinguishing
  a bandwidth-bound regime from a bubble, load-imbalance, or straggler
  problem — real measured runs (this chapter's two cited examples) show
  the bottleneck can shift as configuration changes, and that
  implementation quality, not just theory, determines which strategy
  wins.

### Sources and further reading

Primary sources for this chapter: [@src-17] (the Ultra-Scale
Playbook's "Memory usage in Transformers," "Activation recomputation,"
"Finding the Best Training Configuration," and Appendix A2/A3
sections — the parameter-count and activation-memory formulas, the
per-strategy communication-overlap ratios, the SM-contention caution,
and the multi-thousand-configuration benchmark findings — verified via
full-text extraction of the article's own markdown source),
[@src-54] (the ZeRO paper's Sections 7.1-7.2 — the $2\Psi$/$2\Psi$/$3\Psi$
communication-volume results per stage and the $k\Psi$ notation —
verified via full-text extraction of the arXiv PDF), [@src-52]
(GPipe's Section 2.3 — the re-materialization peak-activation-memory
formula under pipeline partitioning — verified via full-text
extraction of the arXiv PDF), and [@src-53] (Megatron-LM's own
disclosed activation-checkpointing practice and its two-GPU-to-more-GPUs
scaling experiment showing the bottleneck shift from compute to
bandwidth — verified via full-text extraction of the arXiv PDF).
Supporting source: [@src-10] (the arithmetic-intensity/roofline
definition and the nominal-versus-achieved-FLOPs caution — verified via
full-text extraction of the page's own HTML). This chapter does not
reteach what Chapter 4 already covers about *how* DP, ZeRO/FSDP, TP,
SP/CP, PP, and EP replicate, shard, and communicate — only the memory
and communication-cost consequences of those choices. Model-FLOP
utilization, roofline, and distributed-training-specific profiling
tools are introduced only as far as this chapter's diagnosis framework
requires; a dedicated treatment of reading real training-run logs and
dashboards is Chapter 6's subject, not this chapter's.
